background.definition: Atrial fibrillation is a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia characterized by uncoordinated atrial activation and an irregular heart rhythm with consequent deterioration of atrial mechanical function. Atrial flutter is a macroreentrant atrial tachyarrhythmia characterized by an atrial rate of usually 250 to 350 beats/min and varying degrees of atrioventricular block. For purposes of rate control and stroke-prevention treatments, the two are similar; the abbreviation "AF" in this chapter can be understood to refer to both rhythms.

list.listitem: Incidence of atrial fibrillation increases from .1% per year in those younger than 40 years of age to greater than 1.5% per year in women older than 80 years of age and greater than 2% per year in men older than 80 years of age.
The estimated prevalence of atrial fibrillation is about 4% of the general population, increasing to 8% in those older than 80 years of age with the age adjusted prevalence higher among white men.

Prevalence is expected to increase to 5.6 million affected people in 2050 due largely to the aging of the population and increased detection with one trial detecting new AF in 35% of patient with risk factors using an implantable loop recorder over a 3 year period.
The risk of AF was significantly higher in male athletes under the age of 60 years old than compared to the general population.
Perioperative atrial fibrillation is not uncommon in elderly patients, and is a risk factor for future ischemic strokes.
Postoperative (within 30 days of noncardiac surgery) AF has similar stroke risk to nonoperative AF.
AF increases total mortality 2-fold, heart failure 3-fold, and stroke rates 5-fold.
AF is responsible for 15% (nearly 75,000 strokes) of all strokes in the US annually and is the most common cause of disabling strokes among elderly women.
AF can cause "silent" strokes contributing to vascular dementia.
Women over the age of 45 years old with AF reported significantly higher levels of financial stress, traumatic life events, and neighborhood stress.
In patients presenting with an acute myocardial infarction (AMI), older age and increased heart rate on presentation had a higher risk of developing post AMI-AF.

Causes may be primarily cardiac or noncardiac. The cardiac causes of AF include coronary artery disease, hypertension, valvular heart disease (rheumatic and nonrheumatic), dilated cardiomyopathy, and any underlying cause of left atrial dilatation. The noncardiac (usually reversible) causes of AF include any cause of arterial hypoxemia [both acute and chronic (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, COPD; obstructive sleep apnea, OSA)], alcohol use, hyperadrenergic states (hyperthyroidism), pheochromocytoma, theophylline and other stimulant toxicity, hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia.
"Lone" atrial fibrillation accounts for about 10% to 20% of AF and occurs in patients younger than 60 years of age with no identified underlying cardiopulmonary disease.
A meta-analysis found anger, anxiety, and work stress did not increase the risk of AF.
A meta-analysis found that 5% or greater weight gain led to increased the incidence of AF by 13% (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.23, I2=70%).

AF is commonly a result of structural heart disease, for example, diastolic dysfunction of the left ventricle leading to left atrial dilatation, stretch, fibrosis, and subsequent vulnerability to atrial flutter and fibrillation.
Atrial flutter usually occurs from a single reentrant circuit around functional or structural conduction barriers (i.e., the tricuspid valve annulus) within the atria.

Atrial flutter and fibrillation are "interchageable" rhythms; i.e., atrial flutter may degenerate into AF, AF may initiate flutter, or they may "coexist." These rhythms, nonetheless, are not completely identical and treatment modalities (such as radiofrequency ablation) differ depending on whether the patient primarily has atrial fibrillation versus flutter.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Postoperative state such as postcardiac surgery

list.listitem: Screening specifically for atrial fibrillation in asymptomatic adults is not currently recommended. C
Assess risk of stroke in patients with AF using a validated tool such as the CHADS2 or the CHADS2-Vasc score. B
Aspirin is recommended for patients at low risk of stroke, while warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants are recommended for patients at intermediate to high risk of stroke. A

Screening for atrial fibrillation and flutter is not currently recommended by any practice guidelines. The US Preventive Services Task Force continues to concludes that in asymptomatic adults, there is insufficient evidence to recommend screening with electrocardiography for atrial fibrillation.
Screening elderly patients (75 or older) could be considered based on a cohort trial of almost 30,000 patients

Though it is unclear how it predicts future atrial fibrillation, the presence of premature atrial complexes (PACs) on 12 lead electrocardiography is associated with an increased risk of stroke, atrial fibrillation and death versus the absence of PACs.

Smart device-based technology has a variable positive predictive value (34-92%) for dectection of AF, but a more recent 2020 study suggest smart watches may be as good as Holter monitors in high risk patients finding a sensitivity and specificity of 97.3% and 88.6% respectively and a large 2022 study (nearly 456,000 patients) found them to have a high postive predictive value. However, despite these postive trials, a systemic review and meta-analysis calls for more studies with better quality before advising clinicians on their use.

Screening high risk patients with an implantable loop recorder detected 3 times more atrial fibrillation without reducing stroke or systemic arterial embolism risk. Even in patients who had a stroke, inserting an implantable loop recorder did not lead to much benefit compared to usual post stroke care.
Amiodarone and β-blockers, as well as pacing, are options for preventing AF in patients undergoing heart surgery and appear to reduce length of stay.

A randomized trial with 1667 patients found that a strategy of potassium supplementation only when levels fall below 3.6 mEq/L is no worse than tighter control with supplementation at 4.5 mEq/L for preventing atrial arrhythmias following CABG. Additionally, this strategy is cost-saving, eliminates unnecessary clinical interventions, and prevents potential side effects and tolerance issues associated with oral potassium supplementation.
Hypertension and obesity are the two major modifiable risk factors for incidental AF.
Minimizing thromboembolic risk is an important aspect of management of AF. This risk and hence antithrombotic recommendations are identical for atrial flutter and fibrillation.

Depending on the presence of stroke risk factors, the long-term risk for stroke in patients with AF varies from less than 1%/year to greater than 10%/year. See Clinical Decision Rules for decision support tools that help identify patients at low, moderate, or high risk of stroke.

Patients at low risk of stroke are good candidates for aspirin 81 to 325 mg daily. For patients at intermediate to high risk for stroke should be placed on anticoagulation with a DOAC over warfarin unless contraindicated with a target INR of 2 to 3 if warfarin is used.

Excluded from above criteria are patients with reversible causes of AF, pregnant patients, patients with mechanical heart valves or moderate to severe mitral stenosis, and patients with contraindications to antithrombotic therapy.
In patients with chronic, nonvalvular AF, about 10 strokes per 1000 per year are prevented with the use of aspirin and about 25 strokes per 1000 per year are prevented with the use of warfarin.
Diagnosis of AF in the community has to factor in the limitations of ECG reading by primary care physicians and computerized software programs alike. B

A transthoracic echocardiogram is recommended in all patients with AF to determine left atrial (LA) and left ventricular (LV) dimensions and to assess LV wall thickness and function and any underlying cardiopulmonary disease. B

Transesophageal echocardiogram is also recommended to rule out underlying atrial thrombi prior to pharmacological or electrical cardioversion of AF when it has lasted for more than 48 hours or is of unknown duration. A

Differential.Differential_Features: Regular ventricular rate, i.e., constant R-R intervals, "sawtooth" flutter waves
Regular ventricular rate with usually discernible P waves and narrow QRS complexes
Monomorphic or polymorphic P waves, variable P-P intervals, normal QRS complexes

list.listitem: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation: episode is self-terminating, lasts for 7 days or less, usually less than 24 hours; may be recurrent. Most common triggers reported by patients were alcohol (35%), caffeine (28%), exercise (23%), and lack of sleep (21%).
Persistent atrial fibrillation: episode lasts for more than 7 days; may be recurrent and usually implies that a treatment has failed.
Permanent atrial fibrillation: AF has been present more than 1 year, and cardioversion either has not been attempted or has failed.

Pulse palpation is sensitive but not very specific for diagnosis of atrial fibrillation. The absence of A-waves on inspection of the jugular venous pulse is a specific finding for atrial fibrillation. The presence of high frequency waves suggests atrial flutter.
Initial evaluation of a patient with AF involves characterizing the pattern of arrhythmia, determining its cause and defining associated cardiac and extracardiac factors.

Identify risk factors for thromboembolism, using clinical decision rules to categorize patients with atrial fibrillation into low, moderate, and high risk groups for stroke (see Clinical Decision Rules).

In addition to routine ECG and transthoracic echocardiogram for all patients with newly diagnosed AF, initial diagnostic testing may be appropriate to detect other reversible causes, including a metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, pulse oximetry, drug screen, and sepsis work-up.

12 lead ECG in atrial fibrillation: constantly changing R-R intervals and no discernible P waves before the QRS complexes. These are instead replaced by "fine" or "coarse" fibrillation waves. Ventricular rate in untreated AF is usually over 100/min; slow AF may indicate underlying disease of the conduction pathway. Chest leads were somewhat more sensitive but less specific for physician ECG readers.
12 ECG in atrial flutter: typical "sawtooth" pattern of flutter waves with a rapid, regular atrial rate of 250 to 350 beats/min with an atrioventricular block that is usually 2:1 but maybe variable.

Automated devices for home detection of atrial fibrillation have excellent specificity (>98%) but only 67% to 83% sensitivity.A RCT found that in individuals at high risk for AF, a home-based wearable ECG sensor patch resulted in higher rates of AF diagnosis, initiation of anticoagulants, and increased health care resource utilization at 1 year compared to nonmonitored controls.

Transesophageal echocardiogram is recommended if cardioversion is contemplated with atrial fibrillation lasting more than 48 hours or of unknown duration. Notably, many patients are unaware of being in atrial fibrillation, so the duration of atrial fibrillation is often unknown.
The risk of stroke as a result of atrial fibrillation can be estimated with any of several clinical decision rules that have been validated and found to be reliable.

ACC/AHA guidelines recommend using the CHA2DS2-VASc score to assess annual stroke risk in patients with AF. Those with an annual stroke risk < 1% do not require anticoagulation; if 1% to 2% anticoagulation should be considered; and it is strongly recommended if risk is > 2%.
Other validated risk scores include the SPAF score, a risk score based on Framingham data, the van Walraven rule, and a rule intended to identify patients at low risk of stroke while taking aspirin.

Several clinical rules including the HAS-BLED, ORBIT, and ATRIA scores predict the likelihood of bleeding complications. Another clinical rule can predict the likelihood of bleeding in elderly patients started on warfarin.A newer tool can help predict the risk of bleeding for patients on a DOAC

The ABC-Stroke and ABC-Bleeding risk scores (available at Uppsala Research Institute, Sweden: https://www.ucr.uu.se/en/calc4.php?step=1&calc=stroke) integrate age, biomarkers and clinical history to estimate the risk of bleeding and stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation. They have been independently validated and are more accurate than the CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED scores.

The C2HEST risk score can help identify patients at high risk for developing new onset AF. It assigns points as follows: C2: CAD/COPD [1 point each]; H: Hypertension; E: Elderly [Age ≥75, doubled]; S: Systolic HF [doubled]; T: Thyroid disease [hyperthyroidism].

Confirm diagnosis with ECG, and perform careful history and physical to look for secondary causes. Order transthoracic echocardiography to evaluate LA size and blood tests for thyroid, renal, and hepatic function.
Additional tests, as clinically indicated, may include 6-minute walk test, exercise stress testing, holter/event monitoring, transesophageal echocardiography, electrophysiological studies.

Rate control has been shown in single study to be no worse than rhythm control in asymptomatic patients, especially in elderly patients with persistent/recurrent atrial fibrillation and who are at high risk for thromboembolic events. A

A meta-analysis of 14 studies and 193.930 patients found a reduced risk of dementia and cognitive decline in patients treated wtih a rhythm-control strategy versus a rate-control strategy (hazard ratio [HR] 0.74; 95% CI 0.62 - 0.89; I2 = 62%).

A growing body of evidence supports that ablation catheter ablation can be consider as initial treatment or in subjects with symptomatic atrial fibrillation who failed efforts at maintaining sinus rhythm with drug therapy. Those without recurrence after one year can consider discontinuing anticoagulation.A

Most patients with atrial flutter or fibrillation should be anticoagulated with a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) over warfarin, unless contraindicated, regardless of whether a rhythm or rate control strategy is pursued. It should be considered if annual stroke risk is 1% to 2%, and is strongly recommended if > 2% by the CHA2DS2-VASc score.A
Aspirin may be adequate as antithrombotic therapy for patients at low risk for stroke (< 1% annual stroke risk). A
Patients with AF and concomitant stable coronary artery disease do not benefit from adding an antithrombotic to a DOAC.B
Weight loss is recommended in overweight or obese AF patients to reduce symptom burden and severity, and the number and duration of AF episodes.A
AF patients undergoing coronary artery stenting, dual therapy with a P2Y12 inhinitor and a DOAC is a reasonable option to reduce the risk of bleeding. A
Percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion appears safe for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation with a low annual stroke rate. A
Initial management of atrial flutter and fibrillation is similar and dependent on the hemodynamic status of the patient.

Most patients in atrial fibrillation should be anticoagulated with appropriate dosing. ACC/AHA guidelines (2024) recommend evaluating the risk of stroke using the CHA2DS2-VASc score. For patients with an annual stroke risk of 1% to 2% anticoagulation should be considered, and it is strongly recommended if the risk is greater than 2%. They recommend a standard dose of a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) over vitamin K antagonists like warfarin. The exceptions are patients who take a CYP3A4/p-glycoprotein–inducing agent (including azoles, macrolides, and some calcium channel blockers), those with moderate to several mitral stenosis, and those with a mechanical heart valve for whome warfarin is still recommended with an INR goal of 2 to 3. For patients who are low risk (annual stroke risk < 1%, for example, younger than 65 years and without any risk factors for stroke) anticoagulation is not recommended. The guidelines also do not recommend aspirin or aspirin plus clopidogrel for these patients unless there is another indication, such as coronary heart disease.

Hemodynamically unstable patients, as defined by the presence of angina, decompensated heart failure, hypotension, pulmonary edema, or evidence of organ malperfusion are to be electrically cardioverted using synchronized direct current.

Treatment options for the management of hemodynamically stable patients include rate control using atrioventricular (AV) nodal blocking agents or rhythm control using pharmacological or electrical cardioversion.

Patients with minimal symptoms may initially be treated with oral short-acting preparations for ease of dose administration and then converted to an appropriate dose of an extended-release preparation once their ventricular rate is controlled. Acutely symptomatic patients may be started on IV formulations of one of the rate/rhythm controlling drugs that can later be converted to an extended-release oral preparation.

The advantages of restoration of sinus rhythm, by either pharmacological or electrical means, are a return of the heart to normal functioning, symptom relief, and prevention of progressive atrial remodelling associated with persistent AF

A randomized trial identified 4012 patients with subclinical (device or monitor detected and asymptomatic) atrial fibrillation. There was approximately 1 fewer ischemic stroke and 1 more major bleed for every 250 persons treated with apixaban instead of low-dose aspirin. The overall risk of stroke was approximately 1%, which is lower than that for patients with persistent atrial fibrillation and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 3 or higher.

In a single study, rate control has been shown to be not inferior to rhythm control in asymptomatic elderly patients with persistent/recurrent atrial fibrillation and who are at high risk for thromboembolic events. The same is true for patients with atrial fibrillation and concomitant heart failure.

The recommended ventricular rate has traditionally been 60 to 80 bpm at rest and less than 110 bpm with daily activities. However, a recent nonblinded RCT found fewer adverse outcomes and no change in symptoms or hospitalizations in patients randomized to more lenient control (target HR <110 at rest).

A prospective cohort study with 972 patients concluded that participants in the rate control group were more likely to be cognitively impaired 2 years later (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.12-1.98). A meta-analyis of 14 studies (2 randomized trials, 1 case-control study, and 11 cohort studies) with 193,830 participants found an association with a lower risk of incident dementia among adults treated with rhythm control. Nonrandomized study designs all suffer from common biases, including the inability to address channeling effects, confounding by indication, and the healthy user phenomenon.

In patients presenting to the emergency room with atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, a meta-analysis found diltiazem to have better efficacy compared to metoprolol without a change in adverse outcomes.

However, a large registry study found that adults with AF who take apixaban or rivaroxaban for stroke prevention are at a significantly increased risk of serious bleeding with the concurrent use of diltiazem compared with metoprolol for rate control (15 additional bleeds per 100 persons over 10 years). The risk is highest in patients taking diltiazem doses higher than 120 mg per day, with HAS-BLED scores of 4 or higher, and taking rivaroxaban compared with apixaban.
See for the commonly used rate-control agents.

Pharmacologic rhythm control can be achieved using class IC (Flecainide, Propafenone), and III (Amiodarone, Sotalol, Dofetilide) drugs. Because of the propensity for proarrhythmic effects, initiation of some antiarrhythmic agents is preferably done in the inpatient setting at the direction of a cardiologist with continuous EKG monitoring, especially in the setting of structural heart disease or LV dysfunction. Disopyramide, quinidine, flecainide, propafenone, amiodarone, dofetilide, dronedarone, sotalol, and metoprolol reduced the risk of recurrent AF after cardioversion.

A 2019 Cochrane review evaluated antiarrhythmics for maintaining sinus rhythm after cardioversion of atrial fibrillation and found variable results with increased proarrhythmic events and no reduction of atrial fibrillation recurrence with some increasing mortality compared to placebo. Notably, with high certainly of evidence, with sotalol had increased mortality compared to placebo or no treatment (NTH 102).

The SAFE-T trial found greater efficacy of amiodarone over sotalol for conversion of chronic AF to normal sinus rhythm; they have, however, also shown a trend toward increased mortality with the active treatment group. Episodic treatment with amiodarone is less effective than continuous therapy. Dronedarone is effective at preventing recurrence of AF at 1 year (NNT = 9) and a lower risk of hospitalization but no difference in mortality.

In high-risk older patients with recent onset AF, an RCT with 2789 adults found that a strategy of rhythm control resulted in fewer cardiovascular deaths (NNT = 333 per year) and fewer strokes (NNT = 333 per year). However, it comes with the prices of more adverse events and complications and a small decrease in health-related quality of life.
A cohort study (n=972) found rhythm over rate control lead to less cognitive impairment in patients older than 65 years old with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or greater over a two year period.
See for the commonly used rhythm-control agents.

Oral anticoagulants are guideline recommendations in AF patients with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or greater in men or 3 or greater in women. One Norwegian study did see some benefit in anticoagulant use in patients with a score of 1 (lower stroke risk at the expense of more major bleeding, but lower overall risk when combing outcomes of ischemic stoke, major bleeding, and mortality).
Observational data of over 59,000 low risk patients suggest a DOAC may have net clinical benefit.

The ABC-Stroke and ABC-Bleeding risk scores (available at Uppsala Research Institute, Sweden: https://www.ucr.uu.se/en/calc4.php?step=1&calc=stroke) integrate age, biomarkers and clinical history to estimate the risk of bleeding and stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation. They have been independently validated and are more accurate than the CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED scores.
In nonvalvular AF patients, DOACs in general are superior to warfarin in preventing strokes and appear at least as safe as warfarin in terms of major bleeding.

For valvular AF, one study found that rivaroxaban was non-inferior to warfarin, but another found warfarin to have a great net benefit in patients with atrial fibrillation associated with rheumatic heart disease.

DOACs may be more cost-effective in patients who have poor adherence (less than 60% of time in range for INR) on warfarinand have been shown to have a similar balance of risk versus harm in patients older than 75 years old when compared to their younger counterparts. DOACs provide a better balance of benefits (preventing stroke or systemic emboli) and harms (major bleeding) than vitamin K antagonists in adults 80 years or older with atrial fibrillation.

Aspirin is adequate for patients at low risk for thromboembolism, although a Cochrane analysis failed to demonstrate a significant reduction of stroke when compared to placebo. An RCT comparing aspirin with aspirin plus clopidogrel found a small benefit of preventing disabling stroke for dual therapy (NNT = 200) but a similar increase in major hemorrhage (NNT = 143).

Over the past fifty years, warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist (VKA), dosed with a target INR of 2 to 3 has been the cornerstone of thromboembolism prevention in AF. When initiating warfarin for those with AF with high risk of thromboembolism, both 5 and 10 mg initiation strategies can be used. More recent studies of dose-titration found no benefit using pharmacogenetic information above standard clinical algorithms.

Dabigatran is an oral direct thrombin inhibitor that was slightly more effective than warfarin (NNT for all cause mortality of 200 over 2 years) in one RCT with over 18,000 AF High risk patients in atrial fibrillation should be anticoagulated.patients, but the cost is higher. In addition, dabigatran use is associated with a small but statistically significant increased risk of acute coronary syndromes (number needed to harm = 250). Other observational studies have found a lower mortality and stroke risk with dabigatran therapy relative to warfarin, but with a higher rate of gastrointestinal bleeding.

Apixaban is a factor Xa inhibitor that was more effective than aspirin alone (dosed 81-324 mg daily) in subjects with atrial fibrillation and at least one risk factor for stroke who were thought to be poor candidates for warfarin therapy (NNT for stroke or embolism of 48 over 1 year).The ARISTOTLE trial found apixaban to be superior to warfarin in reducing stroke/systemic embolism with lower rates of bleeding and mortality.

Rivaroxaban is a factor Xa inhibitor that was found in the ROCKET-AF trial to be non-inferior to warfarin in reducing stroke/systemic embolism and overall rates of bleeding, but had lower rates of intracranial and fatal bleeding.
A meta-analysis of 10 unique retrospective real-world evidence studies found favorable evidence of using apixaban over rivaroxaban in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.
Edoxaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor with similar efficacy as warfarin and possibly less bleeding, although different dosing levels in clinical trials make this comparison less clear.

An RCT with 984 patients for whom standard dose anticoagulation was considered inappropriate randomized them to edoxaban 15 mg daily or placebo. The lower dose of edoxaban is effective in decreasing stroke and systemic embolism in elderly patients with atrial fibrillation when compared with placebo (NNT = 23). Although the difference in major bleeding rates with edoxaban versus placebo did not reach statistical significance, edoxaban use led to higher rates of GI bleeding (NNTH = 83) and clinically significant non-major bleeding (NNTH = 18).
Idarucizumab for dabigatran and Andexanet alfa (recombinant factor Xa) for rivaroxaban and apixaban are approved reversal agents.
For patients with coronary artery disease and atrial fibrillation, rivaroxaban alone is preferred to rivaroxaban plus aspirin.

A 2020 meta-analysis showe no statistical difference in stroke or systemic embolism in obsese patients (BMI >40 or >120 kg) with a DOAC or warfarin use, but did see a lower bleeding rate in the DOAC group. A more recent meta-anlysis from 2024 found no statistical difference in preventing stroke or systemic embolism across the spectrum of BMI's (>18) and body weights (<50 kg), but did also see the lower reduction of major bleeds with a DOAC but this reduction started to decline with higher BMI's. The analysis only had 2902 patients with BMI >40 and when looking at the adjusted hazard ratio for net clinical outcomes for BMI >40, warfain had a more favorable outcome (5.56 vs 7.25 event rate/year, p = 0.02).

A number of risk scores exist to guide discussions around risk of major bleeding on anticoagulation, but one study found anemia to be associated with major bleeding in patients on vitamin K oral anticoagulants.

Adults with AF taking diltiazem and either apixaban or rivaroxaban had a higher risk of serious bleeding than those taking metprolol. The risk is highest in patients taking diltiazem doses higher than 120 mg per day, with HAS-BLED scores of 4 or higher, and taking rivaroxaban compared with apixaban. In those taking more than 120 mg per day there were 15 more major bleeds per 1000 person-years.
Computerized clinical support tools can help guide guideline-based antithrombotic therpy and optimize prescribing.

In patients on a DOAC or a vitamin K antagonists who underwent a transesophageal echo, the DOAC group had a slightly lower pooled prevalence of left atrial thrombosis (1.0% vs 1.4%, pooled OR of 0.66 (0.52-0.84).

A trial randomized patients to early initiation of a DOAC within 4 days of an acute ischemic stroke or delayed initiation at 7 to 14 days. They found no difference in outcomes at 90 days. However, an individual patient meta-analysis with 5441 patients found that for the primary composite outcome of recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), or unclassified stroke at 30 days, the early DOAC group fared better than the later group (2.1% vs 3.0%; odds ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.50 - 0.98). For individual outcomes, early DOAC initiation decreased the risk of recurrent ischemic stroke (1.7% vs 2.6%; P = .029) without increasing the risk of symptomatic ICH (0.4% in both arms).
See for the commonly used anticoagulants.

The novel monoclonal antibody abelacimab has a lower risk of bleeding than rivaroxaban (which is, not coincidentally, the DOAC with the highest bleeding risk). The study was stopped prematurely, which is concerning because a trend was emerging for higher stroke rates in the abelacimab groups. Although the drug received fast-track designation from the FDA in 2022, it still awaits full approval.

A trial randomized 840 adults who had catheter ablation for AF and remained recurrence-free after one year to continued anticoagulation or discontinuation. The primary outcome of a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and major bleeding occurred significantly less often in the discontinue oral anticoagulant group vs the continue oral anticoagulant group (0.3% vs 2.2%; NNT = 53). In addition, both ischemic stroke and major bleeding individually occurred significantly less in the discontinue group.

listitem.strong: Anticoagulation in patients with comorbid atherosclerosis

list.listitem: A Korean study randomized 1040 adults with AF and stable coronary artery disease to edoxaban monotherapy or edoxaban plus low-dose aspirin (62%) or clopidogrel (38%). After 12 months, a composite of vascular events (death, myocardial infarction, stroke, systemic embolization, or unplanned revascularization) and major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding events. After 12 months of follow-up, the primary outcome was significantly less likely in the edoxaban monotherapy group (6.8% vs 16.2%; HR 0.44; 95% CI 0.30 - 0.65; NNT = 11). Most of the net benefit was driven by fewer major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding events with monotherapy (4.7% vs 14.2%; HR 0.32; 0.14 - 0.73; NNT = 10).

A trial randomized 316 adults with AF and stable atherosclerotic disease to anticoagulant plus aspirin or clopidogrel or to anticoagulant alone. The composite of ischemic CV events and bleeding occurred in 17.8% in the combination group and 19.6% of the monotherapy group (P = .64). There was no statistically significant difference in ischemic cardiovascular events (11.1% vs 14.2%; P = .41); however, major and clinically important bleeding occurred more often in the participants who received combination therapy (19.5% vs 8.6%; NNTH = 10).

Many patients continue to take aspirin plus warfarin, although this combination is not recommended. Ask patients on warfarin if they are also taking aspirin and discontinue aspirin if they are unless there is a specific indication (i.e., recent coronary stent implant). According to a metanalysis of RCTs, patients with nonvalvular AF and an indication for low-dose aspirin had a reduction in stroke/systemic embolism (hazard ratio [HR] 0.78; 95% CI 0.67 - 0.91) and vascular death (HR 0.85; 0.76 - 0.93) when treated with a DOAC compared to warfarin.

Device-detected atrial fibrillation (DDAF), also called subclinical atrial fibrillation, is atrial fibrillation detected by an implanted device such as a cardiac monitor or cardioverter defibrillator. A meta-analysis found a decreased risk of ischemic stroke with DOAC treatment (NNT = 100) but an increase in the risk of major bleeding (NNTH = 62). Fatal bleeding, cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality were not significantly different between groups.

A study identified 4012 patients with subclinical atrial fibrillation with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 3 or higher. They were randomized to apixaban 5 mg twice daily or aspirin 81 mg once daily. The primary outcome of stroke or systemic embolism was less likely with apixaban than with aspirin (0.78% vs 1.24% per year; P = .007; NNT = 217), with most of the benefit from fewer ischemic strokes. Major bleeding was significantly more likely with apixaban than with aspirin (1.53% vs 1.12%; P = .04; NNTH = 243).

Gastrointestinal bleeding is a common cause of interrupting or withholding anticoagulation, but a study found no increase risk of recurrent bleeding in subjects where anticoagulation was continued; in addition, subjects continued on anticoagulation had a lower overall mortality at 2 years. Resuming warfarin therapy in patients with atrial fibrillation after an intracranial bleed was associated with a lower risk of stroke than not resuming warfarin, but in both cohorts the risk of mortality at one year is high (25%).
AF patients with a history of a GI bleed were at an increased risk of subsequent major GI bleed but not stroke, intracranial bleeding, or all-cause mortality.

AF patients with a history of nontraumatic intracranial hemorrhage who resumed anticoagulation therapy had reduced risk of thromboembolic events and all-cause mortality without a significant increased risk of recurrent intracranial hemorrhage.

For patients requiring antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation (i.e., a patient with atrial fibrillation and recent coronary stenting), the data overall is trending towards superior outcomes with less bleeding risk a DOAC and P2Y12 inhibitor (“Dual Therapy”) compared to a DOAC/VKA and dual antiplatelet therapy (“Triple Therapy”). One meta-analysis found apixaban + P2Y12 inhibitors to be the preferred regimen with the lowest bleeding risk and no increase in ischemic events. However, one meta-analysis found dual therapy to have significant increase of stent thrombosis (RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.01-2.50; P = 0.04; I2 = 0%) but this needs to be evaluated in further studies.

For patients maintained on oral anticoagulation with needed planned interruption of anticoagulation (i.e., for planned surgery), bridging therapy with heparin is not associated with benefit, and may lead to excess harm from bleeding.

A network meta-analysis evaluated the benefits and harms of anticoagulation in patients who had suffered a spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage. They found a mix of potential benefits and harms. There were fewer ischemic cardiovascular events (4% vs 19%; NNT = 7) with the use of a DOAC, but a concerning increase in all-cause mortality in the single largest trial (NNTH = 9).
Patients with transcatheter aortic valve implantation and an indication for oral anticoagulation, had similar outcomes between DOACs and VKA.

Atrial fibrillation alone places patients at higher risk for cognitive decline, however, the use of anticoagulation reduces the risk of decline independent of the reduction in stroke and TIA. Warfarin and dabigatran showed similar cognitive outcomes over a 2-year period in elder patients with atrial fibrillation.

In AF patients on long term use of anticoagulants, any use of NSAIDs was associated with increased risk of major bleeding, stroke/ systemic embolism, and hospitalization with similar rates of myocardial infarctions.
Elevated von Willebrand factor in AF patients are independently associated with a higher risk of MACEs and all-cause mortality according to a metanalysis.

In a study investigating edoxaban versus warfarin, Latin American patients with AF had higher rates of intracranial hemorrhage and death than non-Latin American patients, but had similar rates of overall major bleeding and stroke/systemic embolism. A meta-analysis of 8943 Latin American patients found that a DOAC is non-inferior to a VKA for stroke prevention.
Patients with renal impairment have higher bleeding risk on anticoagulation , but evidence suggestion DOACs are just as safe and effective.

In hypokalemic patients (potassium ≤4.0 mmol/L), a rapid increase in serum potassium may terminate recent-onset atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter.However, for preventing atrial fibrillation, giving potassium for values below 3.6 mEq/L showed now difference in atrial arrhythmia in post-op patients compared to giving potassium to maintain values above 4.5 mEq/L with rates of atrial arrhythmia being 26.2% and 27.8% respectively.
In Asian patients with AF, treatment with a DOAC over VKA had similar efficacy and a better safety profile.

High quality evidence is lacking to guide treatment of atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response in patients with an acute decompensated heart failure exacerbation. One small study comparing IV metoprolol vs diltiazem in these patients found similar overall adverse events, but the diltiazem worsened heart failure symptoms requiring increased oxygen requirements and inotropic support.

Inhibiting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system decrease risk of incidental and recurrent AF. A study of almost 154,000 hypertensive patients found that those on an ACEi or ARB had decreased risk of incidental and recurrent AF.A study of heart failure patients (n=20,741), found mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists reduced incidental and recurrent AF events.
Surgical measures are an option in patients with permanent AF who do not respond to rate or rhythm control with drugs, in symptomatic younger patients, or as an initial first line option.

ACC/AHA Guidelines suggest that catheter ablation can be consider as initial treatment or in subjects with symptomatic atrial fibrillation who failed efforts at maintaining sinus rhythm with drug therapy with the MAZE procedure being considered if the patient is undergoing cardiac surgery for another reason.

These measures include: ablation of the AV node with placement of a pacemaker, burst or dual-site atrial pacing and implantable atrial defibrillator, Maze procedure (open heart surgery) to interrupt reentrant circuits in the LA, or percutaneous radiofrequency or cryballoon ablation.

A number of research studies has evaluated ablation vs anti-arrhythmic drug therapy and the data suggest ablation is noninferior to anti-arrhythmic drug therapy and has an overall trend for improvement in quality of life, recurrence of AF (NNT = 2), efficacy (NNT = 11), and reduced symptom burden.

In patients with heart failure and AF, CASTLE-AF found catheter ablation to be superior over medical therapy (rate or rhythm control) with an absolute reduction in death or hospitalization for heart failure of 16.1%. Ablation treated patients also had improved systolic function and higher rates of maintained sinus rhythm. Another HF trial found ablation improved outcomes compared amiodarone with recurrent AF more likely in the admiodarone group, as was unplanned hospitalization (31% vs 57%, p <0.001, NNT = 4) and all cause mortality (8% vs 18%, p = 0.04, NNT = 10) at 2 years.

A network meta-analysis of over 67 RCTs and almost 10,000 patients comparing different catheter ablation approaches found pulmonary vein isolation was more efficacious without differences in safety. Adding additional catheter ablation strategies to pulmonary vein isolation further improved efficacy.

In patients with paroxysmal AF and hypertension, combined renal denervation and catheter ablation resulted in significantly lower rates of AF reoccurrence at 12 months when compared with catheter ablation alone with similar complications rates.

Percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) appears safe for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation with a low annual stroke rate (1.4% yearly) with the recent AHA/ACC guidelines saying it’s reasonable to consider in patients who have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation. It is at least as effective as standard warfarin therapy in reducing adverse cardiovascular outcomes (such as stroke) and all cause mortality. A 2020 meta-analysis found favorable outcomes with LAAO with reduction in ischemic stroke and major bleeding.

A trial identified 1600 patients who had catheter ablation for AF and randomized them to implantation of a device that occludes the left atrial appendage or anticoagulation. At 36 months, there were significantly more clinically relevant major or nonmajor bleeds in the anticoagulation group (18.1% vs 8.5%; P < .001; NNT = 10 over 3 years). The left atrial appendage closure was noninferior to oral anticoagulation for the composite efficacy outcome of death, stroke, or systemic embolism (5.3% vs 5.8% for anticoagulation; P < .001 for noninferiority) and for major bleeding events (3.9% vs 5.0%; P < .001).
Electrical cardioversion is associated with improved symptoms with a small increased stroke risk relative to rate control alone.

When AF has persisted for 48 hours or more or is of unknown duration, pharmacologic or electrical cardioversion is associated with a 5% to 7% risk of arterial thromboembolism over the following month. This risk can be lowered to less than 1% by using one of two strategies: (1) therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin to achieve a target INR of 2 to 3 for at least 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after elective cardioversion; or (2) if prompt cardioversion is desired in the unstable patient, therapeutic anticoagulation with IV unfractionated heparin can be initiated and a multiplane TEE performed to rule out LA thrombus. Heparin is then continued until the patient is successfully transitioned to warfarin with a therapeutic INR that is maintained for at least 4 weeks postcardioversion. New strategies employing novel oral anticoagulants are being evaluated.

For patients with recent onset (<36 hours) of symptomatic AF who presented to the emergency department (ED), early cardioversion in the ED vs delayed cardioversion within 48 hours did not result in a difference of achieving sinus rhythm on an electrocardiogram at a 4-week follow up. The delayed group did initially receive treatment with a rate-control medication and experienced more spontaneous conversions to sinus rhythm without increasing the rate of cardiovascular complications. Though early cardioversion via drug-shock or shock-only strategies are considered effective and safe.
Predictors of relapse out of sinus rhythm following cardioversion include longer duration of AF and one or more previous cardioversions.
Weight loss is recommended in overweight or obese AF patients to reduce symptom burden and severity, and the number and duration of AF episodes.
A randomized trial showed that in 140 patients with paroxysmal or persistent atrial fibrillation, abstention from alcohol resulted in a lower likelihood of recurrent AF (53% vs 73%, NNT = 20).

A trial randomized 200 adults to at least one cup of coffee per day or no caffeine intake following cardioversion for AF. Using intention-to-treat analysis, AF or atrial flutter recurrence occurred significantly less often in the caffeine consumption group than in the caffeine avoidance group (47% vs 64%, respectively).
Recurrence is common at some point even in those with paroxysmal AF, so patients are usually on long-term medications for rate or rhythm control.
Exceptions would be those who have undergone surgical measures for cure or those who have not tolerated the medications.
Restoration of sinus rhythm after catheter ablation is not an indication to stop anticoagulation.

Patients with AF with a fast ventricular response, i.e., heart rate more than 100 bpm or those who are hemodynamically unstable should be hospitalized for either rate control or chemical/electrical cardioversion.
An emergency department protocol can prevent hospitalization in otherwise low risk, stable patients.
See previous section on Drug Therapy, and .

Both atrial flutter and fibrillation increase stroke rates; presence of risk factors such as congestive heart failure, hypertension, previous stroke or TIA, advanced age, and diabetes increase the relative risk and are summarized in the CHADS2 score. A
Over a 5-year period, 25% of patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation will progress to persistent atrial fibrillation. B
About two-thirds of hospitalized patients with AF of less than 72 hours duration will convert spontaneously. B
A systematic review of 36 studies with over 200,000 participants compared the prognosis of patients with symptomatic versus asymptomatic AF and found no difference in outcomes.

According to a cohort study, in symptomatic AF patients presenting to the ED with higher levels of serum N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide and high sensitive troponin T was associated with increased mortality at mid-term follow-up (median 23 months (iQr 4–38).

Treating co-morbid conditions in AF patients improves clinical outcomes. A meta-analysis of 6,782 patients found co-morbid conditions are commonly untreated with only 43.1% of patients with diabetes mellitus meeting guideline directed therapy. Lower mortality was seen in heart failure and slowed AF progression was seen in obstructive sleep apnea patients where guideline directed therapy was followed.
In AF patients, elevations in red cells distribution width was associated with increased CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED and all cause mortality.
Patients who develop new-onset atrial fibrillation in the setting of noncardiac critical illness have higher inhospital and long-term mortality.
Biomarkers exist that can help determine who is likely to attain sinus rhythm
Proteomic biomarkers shows potential for risk stratification in AF over traditional tools.

The choice of using warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants in the elderly for stroke prevention should take into account patient frailty as cognitive impairment and frailty were associated with major bleeding.
Any of the AV nodal blocking agents can be used for rate control in pregnant patients with AF.
Risk stratification for stroke is similar to that in the nonpregnant patient.
Subsequent antithrombotic therapy is chosen according to the stage of pregnancy and risk for stroke.

Those at high risk for thromboembolism may be administered unfractionated heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin (limited data available) during the first and last trimester and oral anticoagulant such as warfarin during the second trimester.

feature.caption: Rate Control Agents for Atrial Flutter or Fibrillation.
feature.feature_body:
Drug (AV Nodal Blocking Agents) Dose Advantages Disadvantages
Digoxin Loading: .25-.5 mg IV Q 6-8 h for 2-3 doses; Maintenance: .125-.5 mg PO daily Positive inotropic effect with LV dysfunction/congestive heart failure Slow onset of action in the acute setting; watch for signs of digitalis toxicity, especially with renal dysfunction
β- Blockers (Metoprolol, Atenolol, Nadolol) Metoprolol: Initial 5 mg IV Q 2 min up to 3 doses; Maintenance: 100 mg PO BID Preferrable in patients with ischemic heart disease, high sympathetic tone Avoid in asthma and COPD
Calcium-channel blockers (Diltiazem, Verapamil) Diltiazem: Initial loading dose of.25 mg/kg (20 mg) IV, may repeat. 35 mg/kg i.v. (25 mg) if necessary followed by infusion rate of 5-15 mg/h for 24 hours, then convert to PO maintenance dose Verapamil: Initial 2.5-10 mg IV slowly; Maintenance: 80-120 mg PO TID-QID Lowers peripheral vascular resistance; useful with elevated blood pressures and angina Negative inotropic effects in LV dysfunction
Adapted from European Heart Rhythm Association, Heart Rhythm Society, Fuster V, Ryden LE, Cannom DS, et al. ACC/AHA/ESC 2006 guidelines for the management of patients with atrial fibrillation. J Am Coll Cardiol 2006;48:854–906.

feature.caption: Pharmacologic Cardioversion of Atrial Flutter/Fibrillation.
feature.feature_body:
Drug Indications and Route of Administration Dose Potential Adverse Effects
Amiodarone Useful in the setting of acute ischemia, MI or LV dysfunction, for both atrial flutter and fibrillation Route: Oral or IV 5-7 mg/kg over 30-60 min, then 1.2-1.8 g per day continuous i.v. or in divided oral doses until 10 g total, then 200-400 mg/d maintenance Slow onset and long half-life; bradycardia, hypotension, pulmonary, liver, optic nerve and thyroid toxicity
Dofetilide Slightly more effective for atrial flutter than for fibrillation Route: Oral 125-500 mcg BID Adjust dose for renal function, body size, age; QT prolongation, torsades de pointes
Flecainide More effective for recent onset AF than for flutter Route: Oral or IV 1.5-3.0 mg/kg over 10-20 min; 200-300 PO Hypotension, rapidly conducting atrial flutter; avoid in LV dysfunction or coronary artery disease
Propafenone Most effective for recent onset AF Route: Oral or IV 1.5-2.0 mg/kg over 10-20 minutes; 450-600 mg PO Hypotension, rapidly conducting atrial flutter; avoid in LV dysfunction
Quinidine Usually administered PO after rate control achieved .75-1.5 g in divided doses over 6-12 h GI upset, hypotension, QT prolongation, torsades de pointes
Procainamide Less effective than others; used for AF 24 h onset Route: Oral or IV Load: 17-50 mg/kg; Maintenance: 2-5 mg/min Hypotension
Sotalol Used more for maintenance of sinus rhythm than for cardioversion 80-320 mg PO BID
Adapted from European Heart Rhythm Association, Heart Rhythm Society; Fuster V, Ryden LE, Cannom DS, et al. ACC/AHA/ESC 2006 Guidelines for the Management of patients with Atrial Fibrillation. J Am Coll Cardiol 2006;48:854–906.
